items.title: @TheOtherYes @danysvnt In democratic societies, everyone has *some* responsibility on how the use of...
items.content:
@TheOtherYes @danysvnt In democratic societies, everyone has *some* responsibility on how the use of  technology maximizes benefits and minimizes bad side effects. 
The benefits of AI are real today, and will greatly expand in the future. 
The bad side effects have, so far, been minimal. 
It's on all of us to make sure it remains that way.

The catastrophe scenarios (extinction, employment apocalypse, etc) are totally ridiculous for anyone who understands how thing work in the real world.
And the p(doom) estimates are all pulled out of their authors' back ends. It makes no sense to attribute a probability to events over which we have complete agency. Whatever probability you come up with merely reveals your lack of confidence that your fellow humans will do the right thing. Confidence in humanity is one thing Geoff and I disagree on.
The other thing we disagree on is the primacy of intelligence. In the real world, intelligence is not synonymous with power and dominance. A virus, a poisonous snake, or a tiger can bring down a human. Lots of very stupid humans dominate much smarter ones (just look at the international political scene). 

Superintelligent AI will work for us and do our bidding, subject to safety guardrails.
It will have no desire to take over.

I have made detailed technical proposals for AI architectures that can be made safe by satisfying safety guardrails at inference time.
I call it Objective-Driven AI Architecture.

items.content: @ChrSzegedy I shouldn't need to spell that to you, but what matters with computation is what the computation does (e.g. what it is trained to do or programmed to do), not its substrate, which is fungible. Transformers are a generic computing substrate. Once upon a time they were trained to be transductive, resulting in zero fluid intelligence, and now they are trained to be inductive, resulting in substantial fluid intelligence. "The substrate is old" is about as interesting of a point as "systolic arrays are from the 1980s" or "transistors are from the 1940s". LRMs are a *new idea* from 2024, implemented on top of an older computing substrate, which is how things usually go

items.content:
Getting tired of panicky doomer posts like the one below, which are becoming widespread, and starting to feel formulaic.

Folks in this genre often point to unnamed critics, and ideas from years ago, and make it sound like all skeptics have exactly the same views, which is very much untrue. For example, I never called AI a con, so he goes after those that did, and not my more nuanced views.)

These posts must sell a lot of subscriptions.

But my advice is don’t panic, and don’t listen panicky merchants of doom.

The reality is that the original pure LLMs were deeply troubled, and it was right to critique them, then.  But of course the field has evolved in four years.

Important some new techniques beyond pure LLMs have been developed (primarily neurosymbolic, along lines I always pushed for). 

But even so, what we have now is heavily dependent on verifiability—a technique that works well for math, and coding, but lacks generality. It’s not superintelligent, it’s super good at math and logic. (Pure LLMs remain poor at both, but symbolic techniques are helping pick up the slack.)

The biggest problem is not that the machines are getting smarter, and that we are getting dumber. 

How so? By stupidly putting systems that are still unreliable in charge of things like air traffic control, and not regulating them, and giving them too much access to the internet.

The real problem with panicky doomers is that they just don’t understand (or pay attention) to critical questions about how different kinds of AI systems actually work.

If you think that a giant LLM is the same thing as Claude Code, for example, you just don’t know what’s going on.

Folks, if we want to make the right policies and predictions and so forth, we can’t treat every goddamn model as a black box.

Learn some AI, if you want to talk about it.

items.title: The 🗝️ fact:  You can’t understand contemporary AI unless you can appreciate the difference between ...
items.content:
The 🗝️ fact:  You can’t understand contemporary AI unless you can appreciate the difference between a model (that is part of a system) and a system as a whole.

If a system as a whole includes both neural networks and symbols, it is by definition neurosymbolic.

To think otherwise is like thinking that an engine IS a car, rather than a component of a car. You can’t make a car out of engines alone. and you can’t (in most cases) make robust, reliable AI systems out of neural networks alone.

Instead, in many domains you get better results by  *integrating* both neural networks and symbols. (Math, where e.g., Lean checks and sometimes rejects the work of LLMs is a good example of this; so is Claude Code).

That was literally the point of my 2001 book The Algebraic Mind and has been a central point throughout my career.

For a long time, people like @GeoffreyHinton argued otherwise, suggesting that all we needed were neural networks by themselves, and that symbols were an archaic waste of time. Hinton likened symbols to “aether”, as if they were complete scientific mistake.

He was wrong. Systems like Claude Code depend heavily on combining neural networks with things like rules, code interpreters, functions, conditionals and loops - all symbolic constructs drawn from classical AI. Math systems use automated theorem provers, which flow directly from Newell and Simon’s symbolic work in the 1950s.

Symbols weren’t a mistake; they were vital, just as neural networks are.  Scaling helped, but by itself it wasn’t enough; symbolic tools and code interpreters and harnesses are now a central part of most working systems.

Neurosymbolic AI has won, overwhelmingly; the pure neural networks that the dogmatists like Hinton used to argue for have been almost entirely displaced by neurosymbolic hybrids.

As @fchollet has also noted, to pretend otherwise is just silly.

This is apparently all from the video of the webcast. When I asked for sources, Claude replied: 

"what the recreation was built from:

SpaceX’s official webcast replay of Flight 15 (YouTube): seconds 74 to 116 drive the timing, camera shots and catch moment, and it’s the footage in the side-by-side and the comparison video.
Wikipedia’s “SpaceX Starship (spacecraft)” article: the ship’s layout for the blueprint view, including tanks, header tanks, downcomers, pressure bottles and engines.
Guinness World Records: the 146 m tower height.
Community cut-away drawings: which way the tank domes bulge.

Everything else is estimated, including heights along the hull, tank sizes, pipe routing and catch rail height. No SpaceX engineering drawings were used."

A free online book: Algebraic Topology for Data Scientists by Michael S. Postol (2023).

Algebraic Topology for Data Scientists is a textbook for readers in data science, computer science, analytics, and related fields who want to understand how topology can describe data, including readers without prior training in algebraic topology.

The central subject is topological data analysis (TDA): using algebraic descriptions of shape and connectivity to complement conventional data and machine-learning methods.

The book first develops the language of spaces, continuous maps, algebraic structures, simplicial complexes, and homology, then uses that groundwork to explain persistent homology.

Readers encounter ways to represent persistence, assess stability, and turn topological summaries into numerical features for tasks such as clustering and classification.

The treatment connects these ideas to point clouds, sublevel sets, graphs, and time series, with examples that include multivariate time-series analysis and classification of internet-of-things data. It also surveys related methods and applications, including Q-analysis, sensor coverage, Mapper, simplicial sets, and UMAP.

@rutgerbregman You can cherrypick and misrepresent all you like, if you want.

I was wrong on revenue, but right that profits would be elusive, and my logic was correct: there was no technical moat, so price wars came, and competition increased. You don’t credit that part of what I was correct on, because it is characteristic of the stance you have taken. And I was definitely wrong on the timign of the bubble collapse (but the logic that I laid out is starting to be recognized widely, and these companies have lost about a quarter of their value already, as people have recognized that, but of course you won’t credit me for any of that.)

You  still don’t credit my years of advocating for regulation, even I pointed out directly. That’s just plain biased of you.

You still don’t credit that I correctly anticipated that neurosymbolic would change things. Or even that I expressed some optimism in 2022 that would eventually happen. 

Pure scaling DID reach a point of diminishing returns. I was CORRECT about that. The fact that you don’t know that suggests you don’t understand what has happened behind the scenes. Nobody is doing pure scaling any more.

If you take away all the  (neuro)symbolic additions (harnesses, tools, loops, conditionals, code interpreters etc) and giant big models on their own would not be that great. You don’t credit that either.

Lastly, Pure LLMs (which was always the target of my critique) DID NOT master math. What mastered math was a NEUROSYMBOLIC hybrid, in which LLMs generate solutions, many flawed, and symbilc systems like Lean verify them. This supports the position that I had all along. But for whatever reason you just continuously ignore the difference between a pure LLM (which was what I critique) and neurosymbolic systems (which was what I advocated), and when the thing I pushed for turns out to be correct, you act like you don’t understand the difference. If you don’t understand it, go learn it. 

Claude Code literally wouldn’t exist without neurosymbolic AI.

All you are doing is cherrypicking and misrepresentation with a large helping of failing to understand the basic architectural distinction between a pure LLM and a hybrid, which is what my entire career has been about.

 I can’t tell if you are being intellectually dishonest, or you don’t understand the issue, or being too lazy, but one thing I can say for certain is that you are *grossly* misrepresenting my body of work as a whole.

items.content:
A free open book: How Search Decides What You See by Aaron Tay Chee Hsien (2026).

Starting with Boolean retrieval, the book shows how text analysis and inverted indexes make explicit search conditions work, then contrasts Boolean eligibility with ranked lexical retrieval, especially BM25.

It builds from these foundations toward learnt representations and dense retrieval, explaining how model training shapes what a system treats as a useful match. It then places single-vector retrieval alongside learnt sparse methods, token-level comparison, reranking, result diversification, and fusion of ranked lists.

Across these topics, the book repeatedly distinguishes a representation from a scoring method, a retrieval stage from a ranking stage, and a product label from evidence about the machinery underneath.

A free online book The Art of EyeProlog: ISO Prolog with Inspectable Proofs by Jos De Roo (2026).

Prolog (short for Programming in Logic) is a declarative logic programming language created in 1972 by Alain Colmerauer and Philippe Roussel. Unlike traditional imperative languages (such as Python or C++) where you write step-by-step instructions on how to solve a problem, Prolog lets you define what is true using formal logic, leaving the language's built-in engine to figure out the solution.

The Art of EyeProlog is a book for readers learning logic programming and for Prolog programmers who want a precise account of EyeProlog’s ISO profile, extensions, and proof facilities.

It assumes no prior Prolog experience for its main instructional route, though readers can skip ahead if they already know the language.

The central subject is Prolog as both a declarative language for stating relations and an operational system that searches for proofs.

Starting with facts, terms, variables, unification, rules, and recursion, the book builds toward lists, arithmetic, finite search, negation, aggregation, and structured data.

The book encourages working alongside a running interpreter and predicting, inspecting, and explaining results. Its complete programs, outputs, proofs, exercises, and laboratories support hands-on study.

A free online book The Science of Computing by Victor Eijkhout, Edmond Chow, and Robert van de Geijn (2022).

The book is aimed at readers studying computational methods and high-performance computing.

The material connects mathematical models, numerical methods, and the performance of computer programs. It introduces partial differential equations through physical examples involving heat flow, distinguishing time-dependent behavior from steady states and relating these models to boundary-value problems. 

Taylor series supplies a mathematical tool for approximating functions and reasoning about the accuracy of numerical methods.

Later project work shifts attention to computer memory: readers simulate caches, examine the hit-and-miss behavior of code, and investigate why growing differences between processor and memory speeds affect performance.

The book’s approach combines mathematical explanation with practical investigation. It motivates equations from physical processes, presents a theorem and its error term as a basis for understanding approximations, and assigns projects that require simulation, analysis, or literature research.
